scenes.onScreen: total.py: a running total of 1 to 5
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Start the total at zero, before the loop. [HL 2] A loop over one to five. [HL 3] Each round adds n to the total. Total becomes total plus n. [HL 4] After the loop, print the final total. The key rule is that the starting line sits outside the loop. If it is inside the loop, the total resets every round.

code.source:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 6):
    total = total + n
print("Sum:", total)

scenes.onScreen: The name total tied to the int 15 after the loop
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the end state. Total is tied to the int fifteen. N is tied to five, the last value in the loop. During the loop, total moved from zero to one, three, six, ten, and fifteen. Each addition made a brand new int, and the tag total moved to it. The accumulator pattern is simply, make a new total from the old one.

Three: A flag starts False and is set True when something is found. Four: Start each of them before the loop, never inside it. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: resetting the total inside the loop
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We add one, two and three, and expect six. The program prints three. Why? The line total equals zero is inside the loop, so every round wipes the total clean. Only the last number is left. Move the starting line above the loop, and the total can grow. No error appears, so watch for this one.

props.wrongCode:
for n in range(1, 4):
    total = 0
    total = total + n
print(total)
props.fixedCode:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total = total + n
print(total)
props.why: Setting total to zero inside the loop wipes the running total at the start of every round, so only the last number survives.

shorts.title: The accumulator
shorts.hook: "The accumulator is the most useful loop pattern."
shorts.script: The accumulator is the most useful loop pattern. You start a total at zero, before the loop. Inside the loop, you add to it every round. When the loop ends, the total holds the answer. One plus two plus three plus four plus five gives fifteen. Remember the rule, the starting line goes outside the loop, never inside. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Add up in a loop.

shorts.title: The counter
shorts.hook: "A counter counts how many items pass a test."
shorts.script: A counter counts how many items pass a test. Start the count at zero. Inside the loop, test each item. If it passes, add one to the count. At the end, the count tells you how many passed. For example, how many numbers up to twenty divide evenly by three? A counter says six. It is the pattern behind every, how many, question. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Count the matches.

shorts.title: The flag
shorts.hook: "A flag is a name that starts as False."
shorts.script: A flag is a name that starts as False. Inside the loop, you set it to True if you find something special. Once True, it stays True. After the loop, you check the flag, and you know whether anything was found. Think of a till light that turns on when a special item is scanned. Flags answer, was there any, questions. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Remember what you saw.

shorts.title: Reset trap
shorts.hook: "Here is the bug behind many wrong totals."
shorts.script: Here is the bug behind many wrong totals. You put the line total equals zero inside the loop. Now every round wipes the total clean, and only the last number is left. Python shows no error. You just get the wrong answer. Move the starting line above the loop, and the total can grow properly. Check this first when a sum looks too small. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Start outside.
